verses.zh: 提幔人以利法回答说：
verses.en: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
verses.commentary:
22:1 "Eliphaz" Eliphaz
has spoken previously in Job 4:1-5:27 and 15:1-35. Apparently he is
reacting to Job's response, which is recorded in Job 21. These three
comforters of Job continue to assert the traditional theology that the
righteous will be blessed and the wicked will be punished in this life
(i.e., the two ways).

See chart of the three cycles of dialogues in Contextual Insights A. of chapter 20.

verses.zh: 人岂能使　神有益呢？智慧人但能有益于己。
verses.en: “Is it to God that a strong man is of benefit?Is it to him that even a wise man is profitable?[NOTE:1]
notes: The third and final cycle of speeches now begins with Eliphaz’ final speech. Eliphaz will here underscore the argument that man’s ills are brought about by sin; he will then deduce from Job’s sufferings the sins he must have committed and the sinful attitude he has about God. The speech has four parts: Job’s suffering is proof of his sin (2-5), Job’s sufferings demonstrate the kinds of sin Job committed (6-11), Job’s attitude about God (12-20), and the final appeal and promise to Job (21-30).
verses.commentary:
22:2-4 This contains a series of
questions which expect a "no" answer. In effect, Eliphaz is
accusing Job of sin. The theological irony is that every one of them is
really an affirmation (Jerome Bible Commentary, p. 524), not only
of God, but also of Job.

The Hebrew of Job 22:2-4 is difficult. John H. Walton suggests that Job

22:2 is another allusion to a "mediator" (cf. The NIV
Application Commentary, Job,
pp. 450-453). If this is true, Eliphaz is suggesting to Job that his law
case (cf. Job 22:4b) against God cannot be helped by any intermediary
(cf. Job 16:19; 19:25-27) and not asserting that God is not affected by
human innocence.

verses.zh: 你为人公义，岂叫全能者喜悦呢？你行为完全，岂能使他得利呢？
verses.en: Is it of any special benefit[NOTE:1] to the Almightythat you should be righteous,or is it any gain to himthat you make your ways blameless?[NOTE:2]
notes: Some do not take this to be parallel to the first colon, taking this line as a statement, but the parallel expressions here suggest the question is repeated.
The word חֵפֶץ (khefets) in this passage has the nuance of “special benefit; favor.” It does not just express the desire for something or the interest in it, but the profit one derives from it.
verses.commentary:
22:3 "Is there any pleasure to the Almighty if you are righteous" This
is exactly what Job 1:8-9 and 2:3-4 assert. The author is alluding to the dialogue between
YHWH and the accuser.

The term "Almighty" is the ancient name for God, Shaddai,
which shows the patriarchal setting (i.e., Abraham's time, the second
millennium B.C.) for the book of Job.

SPECIAL TOPIC: The SHADDAI

For "righteous" see
SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS.

verses.zh: 岂是因你敬畏他就责备你、审判你吗？
verses.en: Is it because of your piety[NOTE:1] that he rebukes youand goes to judgment with you?[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb תַתֵּם (tattem) is the Hiphil imperfect of תָּמַם (tamam, “be complete, finished”), following the Aramaic form of the geminate verb with a doubling of the first letter.

The word “your fear” or “your piety” refers to Job’s reverence—it is his fear of God (thus a subjective genitive). When “fear” is used of religion, it includes faith and adoration on the positive side, fear and obedience on the negative.
verses.commentary:
22:4 "Is it because of your reverence that He reproves you,

That He enters into judgment against you" Again, this verse,
along with Job 22:8, asserts the traditional theology. In their understanding, Job's problem had to
be one of unconfessed sin. Their theology was so tightly encapsulated that no other options were available.

The term "reverence" (BDB 432) is literally "fear."
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT).

verses.zh: 你的罪恶岂不是大吗？你的罪孽也没有穷尽；
verses.en: Is not your wickedness great[NOTE:1] and is there no end to your iniquity?
notes: Of course the point is that God does not charge Job because he is righteous; the point is he must be unrighteous.
verses.commentary:
22:5-9 This is an extended list
of supposed sins that Job has secretly committed but which he will not
confess. It is interesting that all of these sins (i.e., "great
wickedness," and "iniquities without end," Job 22:5) are
those which the rich commit against the poor. Job defends himself
against these charges in Job 31:16-23.b

- taken pledges of your brothers without cause (cf. Job 24:3,9; Exod. 22:26-27;
Deut. 24:6,10-13,17; Ezek. 18:7,12,16)

- stripped clothing from the poor (cf. Job 31:19,20; Deut. 24:17)

- given no water to the weary

- withheld bread (food) from the hungry (cf. Job 31:16,17,31; Isa. 58:7,10)

- sent widows away empty (cf. Job 24:3,21; 29:13; 31:16,18; Deut. 24:17)

- crushed the strength of the orphans (cf. Job 6:27)

- Job 22:8 is another charge; Job has used his wealth, position to defraud the
poor and helpless (cf. TEV, NJB)

This list of social atrocities is from

- ANE culture in general

- a knowledge of the Mosaic Law

I continue to think that Job was written by a sage at the Judean court,
using the history of a long dead, famous person from Edom. These
dialogues were never spoken by real persons (people in the ANE did not
speak to each other in poetic imagery and parallelism). These dialogues
reveal truth much like the Gospel of John (but in it real people are
speaking) uses dialogues (i.e., 27 of them) to reveal truth about the
person and work of Christ. Be careful of linking a view of history with
a view of inspiration. God has chosen many literary forms to truly
reveal Himself! These forms would have been quickly identified by
contemporary hearers/readers.

verses.zh: 因你无故强取弟兄的物为当头，剥去贫寒人的衣服。
verses.en: “For you took pledges[NOTE:1] from your brothers for no reason,and you stripped the clothing from the naked.[NOTE:2]
notes: The adjective רַבָּה (rabbah) normally has the idea of “great” in quantity (“abundant,” ESV) rather than “great” in quality.
The verb חָבַל (khaval) means “to take pledges.” In this verse Eliphaz says that Job not only took as pledge things the poor need, like clothing, but he did it for no reason.

verses.zh: 困乏的人，你没有给他水喝；饥饿的人，你没有给他食物。
verses.en: You gave the weary[NOTE:1] no water to drinkand from the hungry you withheld food.
notes: The “naked” here refers to people who are poorly clothed. Otherwise, a reading like the NIV would be necessary: “you stripped the clothes…[leaving them] naked.” So either he made them naked by stripping their garments off, or they were already in rags.

verses.zh: 有能力的人就得地土；尊贵的人也住在其中。
verses.en: Although you were a powerful man,[NOTE:1] owning land,[NOTE:2] an honored man[NOTE:3] living on it,[NOTE:4]
notes: The term עָיֵף (ʿayef) can be translated “weary,” “faint,” “exhausted,” or “tired.” Here it may refer to the fainting because of thirst—that would make a good parallel to the second part.
The idiom is “a man of arm” (= “powerful”; see Ps 10:15). This is in comparison to the next line, “man of face” (= “dignity; high rank”; see Isa 3:5).
Heb “and a man of arm, to whom [was] land.” The line is in contrast to the preceding one, and so the vav here introduces a concessive clause.
The expression is unusual: “the one lifted up of face.” This is the “honored one,” the one to whom the dignity will be given.
verses.commentary:
22:8 "the earth" This Hebrew word (BDB 75) has a wide semantic field. Here it
should be "land" (JPSOA) or "family fields." See

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH (OT).

The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1533) mentions that the DSS MS of Job, from
Cave 11, sees this verse as an allusion by Eliphaz to Job's comments in
Job 9:24.

verses.zh: 你打发寡妇空手回去，折断孤儿的膀臂。
verses.en: you sent widows away empty-handed,and the arms[NOTE:1] of the orphans you crushed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Many commentators simply delete the verse or move it elsewhere. Most take it as a general reference to Job, perhaps in apposition to the preceding verse.
The “arms of the orphans” are their helps or rights on which they depended for support.

verses.zh: 因此，有网罗环绕你，有恐惧忽然使你惊惶；
verses.en: That is why snares surround you,and why sudden fear terrifies you,
verses.commentary:
22:10-11 These verses show the result (i.e., "therefore," BDB 485) of
such actions toward the socially disadvantaged. They express a wish for God's justice!

- snares surround you

- sudden dread terrifies you (cf. Job 18:8-11)

- darkness comes upon you, so dark you cannot see (i.e., like the Egyptian plague of
Exod. 10:21-23; also note Job 5:14; 12:25; 15:30; 18:18; 20:26, some of which is imagery
of problems and confusion or death)

- drown in much water

Actions of the elite, powerful, and wealthy toward the socially
ostracized or disempowered have consequences in time and eternity (cf.
Matt. 25:31-46).

verses.zh: 或有黑暗蒙蔽你，并有洪水淹没你。
verses.en: why it is so dark you cannot see,[NOTE:1] and why a flood[NOTE:2] of water covers you.
notes: The verb in the text is Pual: יְדֻכָּא (yedukkaʾ, “was [were] crushed”). GKC 388 §121.b would explain “arms” as the complement of a passive imperfect. But if that is too difficult, then a change to Piel imperfect, second person, will solve the difficulty. In its favor is the parallelism, the use of the second person all throughout the section, and the reading in all the versions. The versions may have simply assumed the easier reading, however.

Heb “or dark you cannot see.” Some commentators and the RSV follow the LXX in reading אוֹ (ʾo, “or”) as אוֹר (ʾor, “light”) and translate it “The light has become dark” or “Your light has become dark.” A. B. Davidson suggests the reading “Or seest thou not the darkness.” This would mean Job does not understand the true meaning of the darkness and the calamities.

verses.zh: 神岂不是在高天吗？你看星宿何其高呢！
verses.en: “Is not God on high in heaven?[NOTE:1] And see[NOTE:2] the lofty stars,[NOTE:3] how high they are!
notes: The word שִׁפְעַת (shifʿat) means “multitude of.” It is used of men, camels, horses, and here of waters in the heavens.
This reading preserves the text as it is. The nouns “high” and “heavens” would then be taken as adverbial accusatives of place (see GKC 373-74 §118.g).
The parallel passage in Isa 40:26-27, as well as the context here, shows that the imperative is to be retained here. The LXX has “he sees.”
verses.commentary:
22:12-14 This seems to be the
claim of Eliphaz that Job has misunderstood the transcendent and
all-knowing power of God.

22:12b

NASB
"Look"

NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta, NET
"See"

LXX, TEV, REB
"God. . .look down"

NJB
"does he not see"

The MT has "see" (BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal
IMPERATIVE), which implies that
humans look at the "highest stars," but without changing the
consonants it is possible for the line of poetry to refer to God looking
down on the highest star (TEV, NJB), thereby forming a better parallel
with Job 22:12b (see notes in UBS Text Project, p. 63).

verses.zh: 你说：　神知道甚么？他岂能看透幽暗施行审判呢？
verses.en: But you have said, ‘What does God know?Does he judge through such deep darkness?[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “head of the stars.”
verses.commentary:
22:13 "the thick darkness"
This NOUN (BDB 791) is
associated with theophanies. When God appears to humans, His holiness is
overpowering and even deadly, so He hides Himself in thick clouds (cf.
Exod. 19:9; 20:21; Deut. 4:11; 5:22; 1 Kgs. 8:12; Ps. 18:11; 97:2).

22:14b

NASB, REB, NET
"the vault of heaven"

NKJV, LXX, Peshitta
"the circle of heaven"

NRSV
"the dome of heaven"

NJB
"the rim of the heavens"

JPSOA
"the circuit of heaven"

This is the ancient imagery of the atmosphere above the earth (i.e.,
flat earth) as a dome (hammered metal) or stretched skin (cf. Isa.
40:22).

In this context, the full imagery is God walking on the clouds of heaven
and observing all that happens on earth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

verses.zh: 密云将他遮盖，使他不能看见；他周游穹苍。
verses.en: Thick clouds are a veil for him, so he does not see us,[NOTE:1] as he goes back and forthin the vault[NOTE:2] of heaven.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Eliphaz is giving to Job the thoughts and words of the pagans, for they say, “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?” (see Pss 73:11; 94:11).
Heb “and he does not see.” The implied object is “us.”
The word is “circle; dome”; here it is the dome that covers the earth, beyond which God sits enthroned. A. B. Davidson (Job, 165) suggests “on the arch of heaven” that covers the earth.

verses.zh: 你要依从上古的道吗？这道是恶人所行的。
verses.en: Will you keep to the old path[NOTE:1] that evil men have walked—
notes: The idea suggested here is that God is not only far off, but he is unconcerned as he strolls around heaven—this is what Eliphaz says Job means.
verses.commentary:
22:15 "Will you keep the ancient path" This phrase is usually used for
God's path (cf. Job 23:11; Ps. 139:24; and Jer. 6:16). However, there is a possible Ugaritic
root, glm, that could mean "dark path," which would refer to the path
of the wicked (AB, p. 151). This seems to be more contextually appropriate.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

verses.zh: 他们未到死期，忽然除灭；根基毁坏，好像被江河冲去。
verses.en: men[NOTE:1] who were carried off[NOTE:2] before their time,[NOTE:3] when the flood[NOTE:4] was poured out[NOTE:5] on their foundations?[NOTE:6]
notes: The “old path” here is the way of defiance to God. The text in these two verses is no doubt making reference to the flood in Genesis, one of the perennial examples of divine judgment.
The word “men” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied to clarify the relative pronoun “who.”
The verb קָמַט (qamat) basically means “to seize; to tie together to make a bundle.” So the Pual will mean “to be bundled away; to be carried off.”
The clause has “and [it was] not the time.” It may be used adverbially here.
The word is נָהַר (nahar, “river” or “current”); it is taken here in its broadest sense of the waters on the earth that formed the current of the flood (Gen 7:6, 10).
The verb יָצַק (yatsaq) means “to pour out; to shed; to spill; to flow.” The Hophal means “to be poured out” (as in Lev 21:10 and Ps 45:3).
verses.commentary:
22:16 Notice the stated divine action against those who walk the path of wickedness.

- They die before their time.

- Their legacy and memory are destroyed (i.e., by a great flood of judgment).

Eliphaz is alluding to Job's current condition.

▣ "snatched away"
This VERB (BDB 888, KB 1108, Pual PERFECT)
is found only in Job (twice).

- Job 16:8

- Job 22:16

It implies a personal act of God. It denotes a premature death (cf. Job 20:11; 22:16; Ps.
102:23-24; Isa. 38:10), which showed God's displeasure.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (ANTHROPOMORPHISM)

verses.zh: 他们向　神说：离开我们吧！又说：全能者能把我们怎么样呢？
verses.en: They were saying to God, ‘Turn away from us,’and, ‘What can the Almighty do to us?’[NOTE:1]
notes: This word is then to be taken as an adverbial accusative of place. Another way to look at this verse is what A. B. Davidson (Job, 165) proposes “whose foundation was poured away and became a flood.” This would mean that that on which they stood sank away.
verses.commentary:
22:17-18 These verses are almost
letter for letter a quote from Job 21:14-16, but the exact purpose of
Eliphaz quoting Job is uncertain, unless he is mocking his words.

22:17b

NASB, NKJV, TEV
"do to them"

NRSV, NJB, REB, Peshitta, NET
"do to us"

JPSOA
"do about it"

LXX
"bring against us"

The NASB follows the MT. The NRSV follows the LXX, Syriac, Qumran
Targum. The DSS Targum suggests that "to us" means "for
us," which would link the thought to Job 22:3b. This would reflect
the Accuser's charges in Job 1 and 2 of faith for favors.

verses.zh: 哪知　神以美物充满他们的房屋；但恶人所谋定的离我好远。
verses.en: But it was he[NOTE:1] who filled their houses with good things—yet the counsel of the wicked[NOTE:2] was far from me.[NOTE:3]
notes: The form in the text is “to them.” The LXX and the Syriac versions have “to us.”
The pronoun is added for this emphasis; it has “but he” before the verb.
See Job 10:3.

verses.zh: 义人看见他们的结局就欢喜；无辜的人嗤笑他们，
verses.en: The righteous see their destruction[NOTE:1] and rejoice;the innocent mock them scornfully,[NOTE:2] saying,
notes: The LXX has “from him,” and this is followed by several commentators. But the MT is to be retained, for Eliphaz is recalling the words of Job. Verses 17 and 18 are deleted by a number of commentators as a gloss because they have many similarities to 21:14-16. But Eliphaz is recalling what Job said, in order to say that the prosperity to which Job alluded was only the prelude to a disaster he denied (H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 156).
The line is talking about the rejoicing of the righteous when judgment falls on the wicked. An object (“destruction”) has to be supplied here to clarify this (see Pss 52:6 [8]; 69:32 [33]; 107:42).
verses.commentary:
22:19-20 These two verses
describe the feelings of righteous people at the just judgment that
befalls the wicked. Eliphaz considered himself righteous and Job wicked.

22:20a

NASB, NKJV, NRSV
"adversaries"

LXX, JPSOA, KJV
"substance"

NJB, NET
"enemies"

REB
"riches"

The MT has "adversaries" (קים, BDB 879, KB
1096), but this root is found only here. The parallelism with Job 22:20b
suggests "substance" (possibly, יקום,
BDB 879; an Arabic root, or קנין, BDB 889. "thing
got or acquired").

▣ "fire" The
mention of "fire" and "flood" (Job 22:16) are

- the Jewish sages' knowledge of the Flood of Genesis 6-9 and Sodom and Gomorrah of Genesis 18-19

- general metaphors for judgment in the ANE

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

verses.zh: 说：那起来攻击我们的果然被剪除，其余的都被火烧灭。
verses.en: ‘Surely our enemies[NOTE:1] are destroyed,and fire consumes their wealth.’
notes: In Ps 2:4 it was God who mocked the wicked by judging them.

verses.zh: 你要认识　神，就得平安；福气也必临到你。
verses.en: “Reconcile yourself[NOTE:1] with God,[NOTE:2] and be at peace[NOTE:3] with him;in this way your prosperity will be good.
notes: The word translated “our enemies” is found only here. The word means “hostility,” but used here as a collective for those who are hostile—“enemies.” Some commentators follow the LXX and read “possessions,” explaining its meaning and derivation in different ways. Gordis simply takes the word in the text and affirms that this is the meaning. On the other hand, to get this, E. Dhorme (Job, 336) repoints קִימָנוּ (qimanu) of the MT to יְקוּמַם (yequmam), arguing that יְקוּם (yequm) means “what exists [or has substance]” (although that is used of animals). He translates: “have not their possessions been destroyed.”

The verb סָכַן (sakhan) meant “to be useful; to be profitable” in v. 2. Now, in the Hiphil it means “to be accustomed to” or “to have experience with.” Joined by the preposition “with” it means “to be reconciled with him.” W. B. Bishai cites Arabic and Ugaritic words to support a meaning “acquiesce” (“Notes on hskn in Job 22:21, ” JNES 20 [1961]: 258-59).
Heb “him”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
22:21-22 Eliphaz, with "seeming"
compassion (Job 4-5) and half truths, calls on Job to repent. He
says he cares for Job! His affirmations of God's grace are absolutely accurate
but he insists that Job is under judgment, when in reality he is not.

Note the IMPERATIVES used
as wishes for Job to act in a certain way.

- yield now" – BDB 698, KB 755, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
which denotes an action that is clearly demonstrated, cf. Num. 22:30; Ps. 139:3

- be at peace with Him" – BDB 1023, KB 1532, Qal IMPERATIVE, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)

- receive God's teachings – BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

- establish His words in your heart – BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE

- there is one more action (i.e., IMPERATIVE, BDB 1011, KB 1483) in Job 22:24
which asks Job to renounce all his wealth

The result of confession and repentance will be "good" (BDB
375), Job 22:21b,23,28b,29,30. This has been the message of the three
comforters from the beginning.

verses.zh: 你当领受他口中的教训，将他的言语存在心里。
verses.en: Accept instruction[NOTE:1] from his mouthand store up his words[NOTE:2] in your heart.
notes: The two imperatives in this verse imply a relationship of succession and not consequence.
The Hebrew word here is תּוֹרָה (torah), its only occurrence in the book of Job.
verses.commentary:
22:22 "Please receive instructions from His mouth" It is interesting to
note that this is the only use of the Hebrew word Torah (BDB 435) in all the book of
Job. This also seems to imply that Eliphaz is claiming to speak for God. This is a pitfall that
all of us face from time to time.

Job claims to have received God's word/teaching in Job 23:12. It is the
words of his three comforters he rejects as irrelevant to his situation
(i.e., an innocent man suffering under God's direction or approval).

verses.zh: 你若归向全能者，从你帐棚中远除不义，就必得建立。
verses.en: If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up;[NOTE:1] if you remove wicked behavior far from your tent,
notes: M. Dahood has “write his words” (“Metaphor in Job 22:22, ” Bib 47 [1966]: 108-9).
verses.commentary:
22:23-30 In these verses Job is
offered rewards for his confession and repentance ("If. . .if. . ."
BDB 609). This is exactly the charge that Satan makes to God in the
Prologue of Job. It again sees God's relationship to us on the basis of
"the two ways."

22:23 "return" This is the VERB (BDB 996, KB
1427, Qal IMPERFECT) that denotes "turning"
(i.e., turning from sin and to God).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ "you will be restored"
This is literally "built up" or "be made prosperous"
(בנה, BDB 124, KB 139, Niphal imperfect) but the LXX makes it
a similar root, "humble" (ענה, BDB
776, KB 851, Pual IMPERFECT).

verses.zh: 要将你的珍宝丢在尘土里，将俄斐的黄金丢在溪河石头之间；
verses.en: and throw[NOTE:1] your gold[NOTE:2] in the dust—your gold[NOTE:3] of Ophir among the rocks in the ravines—
notes: The MT has “you will be built up” (תִּבָּנֶה, tibbaneh). But the LXX has “humble yourself” (reading תְּעַנֶּה [teʿanneh] apparently). Many commentators read this; Dahood has “you will be healed.”

Heb “place.”tc The form is the imperative. Eliphaz is telling Job to get rid of his gold as evidence of his repentance. Many commentators think that this is too improbable for Eliphaz to have said, and that Job has lost everything anyway, and so they make proposals for the text. Most would follow Theodotion and the Syriac to read וְשָׁתָּ (veshatta, “and you will esteem….”). This would mean that he is promising Job restoration of his wealth.

The word for “gold” is the rare בֶּצֶר (betser), which may be derived from a cognate of Arabic basara, “to see; to examine.” If this is the case, the word here would refer to refined gold. The word also forms a fine wordplay with בְצוּר (vetsur, “in the rock”).
verses.commentary:
22:24-25 The Hebrew text is in disarray. It is uncertain if Job 22:24 and
25 follow the literary context of Job 22:23 or if these verses show that Eliphaz
is

- encouraging Job to trust in God not in riches

- promising the restoration of wealth (Syriac)

Ophir, mentioned in Job 22:23, is an unknown geographical locality, but
proverbial for its fine gold.

22:25b

NASB
"choice"

NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA
"precious"

TEV
"piled high"

NJB
"piled in heaps"

REB
"in double measure"

LXX
"pure as silver tried by fire"

Peshitta, KJV
"plenty"

This FEMININE PLURAL NOUN
(BDB 419) is used of things "high" or "towering."

- horns – Num. 23:22; 24:8

- peaks – Ps. 95:4

- here, of silver ore possibly in heaps, or stacked up refined bars

verses.zh: 全能者就必为你的珍宝，作你的宝银。
verses.en: then the Almighty himself will be your gold,[NOTE:1] and the choicest[NOTE:2] silver for you.
notes: The Hebrew text simply has “Ophir,” a metonymy for the gold that comes from there.
The form for “gold” here is plural, which could be a plural of extension. The LXX and Latin versions have “The Almighty will be your helper against your enemies.”

verses.zh: 你就要以全能者为喜乐，向　神仰起脸来。
verses.en: Surely then you will delight yourself[NOTE:1] in the Almightyand will lift up your face toward God.
notes: E. Dhorme (Job, 339) connects this word with an Arabic root meaning “to be elevated, steep.” From that he gets “heaps of silver.”

verses.zh: 你要祷告他，他就听你；你也要还你的愿。
verses.en: You will pray to him, and he will hear you,and you will fulfill your vows to him.[NOTE:1]
notes: This is the same verb as in Ps 37:4. G. R. Driver suggests the word comes from another root that means “abandon oneself to, depend on” (“Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 84).

verses.zh: 你定意要做何事，必然给你成就；亮光也必照耀你的路。
verses.en: Whatever you decide on[NOTE:1] a matter,it will be established for you,and light will shine on your ways.
notes: The words “to him” are not in the Hebrew text, but are implied.

verses.zh: 人使你降卑，你仍可说：必得高升；谦卑的人，　神必然拯救。
verses.en: When people are brought low[NOTE:1] and you say,‘Lift them up!’[NOTE:2] then he will save the downcast;[NOTE:3]
notes: The word is גָּזַר (gazar, “to cut”), in the sense of deciding a matter.
There is no expressed subject here, and so the verb is taken as a passive voice again.

The word גֵּוָה (gevah) means “loftiness; pride.” Here it simply says “up,” or “pride.” The rest is paraphrased. Of the many suggestions, the following provide a sampling: “It is because of pride” (ESV), “he abases pride” (H. H. Rowley); “[he abases] the lofty and the proud” (Beer); “[he abases] the word of pride” [Duhm]; “[he abases] the haughtiness of pride” [Fohrer and others]; “[he abases] the one who speaks proudly” [Weiser]; “[he abases] the one who boasts in pride” [Kissane]; and “God [abases] pride” [Budde, Gray].
verses.commentary:
22:29-30 This has proven to be a
very controversial passage because the rabbis and Roman Catholicism have
taken the uncertainty of the Hebrew text and have asserted the doctrine
of the "merit of the saints." This is in direct contradiction
to the message of the book of Job, although Job himself prays for his
three friends at the end of the book, as God instructs him (also note
Abraham's intercession for Sodom/Lot in Gen. 18:21-33; and possibly
Ezek. 14:14,20). This idea that the prayers of a righteous person affect
God is surely true (cf. James 5:16; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER), but this involves
no transfer of merit (cf. Ezekiel 18).

Notice how Job 22:2-4 contradicts the understanding of Job 22:30 related
to "merits" of righteous people!

22:29 This is a good example of
the theological half-truths found in the three comforters' messages.
Much of what they say is accurate.

- God opposes the proud but exalts the humble (OT reversal motif)

- confession and repentance bring restoration and peace with God (Job 22:23-28)

verses.zh: 人非无辜，　神且要搭救他；他因你手中清洁，必蒙拯救。
verses.en: he will deliver even someone who is not innocent,[NOTE:1] who will escape[NOTE:2] through the cleanness of your hands.”
notes: Or “humble”; Heb “the lowly of eyes.”

The Hebrew has אִי־נָקִי (ʾi naqi), which could be taken as “island of the innocent” (so Ibn-Ezra), or “him that is not innocent” (so Rashi). But some have changed אִי (ʾi) to אִישׁ (ʾish, “the innocent man”). Others differ: A. Guillaume links אִי (ʾi) to Arabic ʿayya “whosoever,” and so leaves the text alone. M. Dahood secures the same idea from Ugaritic, but reads it אֵי (ʾe).
verses.commentary:
22:30

NASB, NKJV
"one who is not innocent"

NRSV
"those who are guilty"

RSV
"the innocent man"

TEV
"you are innocent"

NJB
"who is innocent"

JPSOA
"guilty"

LXX, REB, Peshitta
"the innocent"

The textual issue is obvious when you compare RSV with NRSV. The "innocent"
man (RSV, TEV, NJB, REB) follows the ancient versions (i.e., Aramaic Targums,
LXX, Peshitta). The MT has "not" (BDB 22 IV) with "innocent"
(cf. Job 4:7; 9:23; 17:8; 22:19,30; 27:17). However, it is a form of
negation found only in later Hebrew and found nowhere else in the OT (it
is found in Phoenician and Ethiopian, cf. John Walton, NIV
Application Commentary, Job,
p. 246). The parallelism of Job 22:30a and 30b fits best without the
negative. The UBS Text Project (p. 66) gives the MT a "C" rating
(considerable doubt). The committee suggested several possible
translations for אי (BDB 33 IV).

- no/not

- whoever (Arabic root)

- man (add one consonant to "not," RSV)

- God

- island (Ibn Ezra, KJV)

- country (implication of #5)

Notice the word "innocent" is used in a negative sense in Job
22:19b-20.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Is Eliphaz asserting that God is unaffected by human actions in Job 22:2-4?

- Can Eliphaz prove or demonstrate his charges against Job (Job 22:5-9)?

- Is Elihaz accusing Job of believing God is uninvolved in the affairs of humans (Job 22:12-14)?

- What is the "ancient path" or "old path"? How is it different from
"everlasting way" of Ps. 139:24?

- What does Job 22:24 mean?

- Why is Job 22:30 so hard to interpret?
